title: Horizontal effect of the HRA: privacy v the press
subtitle: Two rights collide — Article 8 against Article 10, private party against private party
objectives: Explain how the Human Rights Act achieves indirect horizontal effect through section 6, without creating a free-standing statutory cause of action between private parties
State the two-stage test for the common law tort of misuse of private information, and trace its development from Campbell through Von Hannover (No 2) to ZXC
Apply the Article 8/Article 10 balancing exercise to a new privacy-versus-publication fact pattern

leadingAuthorities.role: Founds the modern tort of misuse of private information from Article 8, balanced against Article 10
Strasbourg's balancing criteria — contribution to a debate of general interest, the claimant's role, prior conduct, content, form and consequences of publication
Modern synthesis: a person under criminal investigation has, as a starting point, a reasonable expectation of privacy in that fact before charge

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students frequently write as though English law has a free-standing 'tort of privacy' created directly by Article 8. Where the profile shows this gap, this note appears: 'You've got the outcome right — this lesson tightens up the mechanism that gets you there.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You can state the doctrine accurately. The test pool below is weighted towards fact patterns: you'll need to run the two-stage test (reasonable expectation, then balancing) rather than just naming it.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and get section 6's mechanism straight before anything else — every later part in this lesson assumes you understand why this is indirect horizontal effect through the common law, not a direct statutory claim.

overview.hook: Two rights, both written into the same Convention, both taken exactly as seriously as each other, pointing in opposite directions at the same photograph. Article 8 says: leave her alone. Article 10 says: you may publish. Neither wins by default, and — this is the twist that trips up most students — neither party in the courtroom is the state. This is a fight between two private parties: a claimant and a newspaper. So how does a treaty binding governments end up deciding a fight between a celebrity and a tabloid? That mechanism is this lesson's real subject, and the story of how the courts built it runs through three cases across two decades.

parts.heading: How a treaty against the state reaches a fight between private parties
parts.voice: two rights collide — opens with the mechanical puzzle before any case law
body: The Human Rights Act's core architecture is vertical: section 6 makes it unlawful for a public authority to act incompatibly with a Convention right, and the obvious defendants are government bodies, police forces, public hospitals. A newspaper is not a public authority. So when a claimant wants to stop a newspaper publishing details of her private life, on what basis can Article 8 possibly reach that dispute at all?

The answer is indirect horizontal effect, and section 6 is still doing the work — just one step removed. Courts are themselves public authorities under section 6. That means a court deciding a private dispute between a claimant and a newspaper must develop and apply the common law compatibly with Convention rights, even though neither party to the case is the state. The Convention doesn't create a new statutory cause of action a claimant can sue on directly against a private defendant; instead, it reshapes an existing common law action so that it gives effect to Convention values.

The vehicle the courts reshaped was the equitable action for breach of confidence. Before the HRA, that action was awkward for privacy claims: it traditionally required some prior relationship of confidence between the parties, which a stranger with a long-lens camera plainly doesn't have. The courts' solution — worked out case by case, and crystallised in the case this lesson turns to next — was to develop breach of confidence into a distinct tort: misuse of private information, freed from the old confidential-relationship requirement and built directly around the Article 8/Article 10 balance.

components.definition: The mechanism by which Convention rights influence disputes between private parties: not through a free-standing statutory right of action, but because courts, as public authorities under s 6 HRA, must develop and apply existing common law causes of action compatibly with Convention rights.

interaction.prompt: A claimant sues a newspaper directly under 'section 8 Article 8 of the Human Rights Act' for invading her privacy. Is this a correct description of how UK privacy law works?
options: No — there is no free-standing statutory cause of action against a private party; the claim is brought in the common law tort of misuse of private information, shaped by Article 8 through the courts' own s 6 duty
Yes — the HRA creates a direct statutory tort of privacy enforceable against any defendant, public or private
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Keep the mechanism precise: the cause of action is a common law tort, not a statutory HRA claim — Article 8 shapes it indirectly, through the court's own duty as a public authority.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — this is the exact error this lesson exists to correct. There is no direct statutory privacy tort under the HRA; the claim is the common law tort of misuse of private information, developed to reflect Article 8 because courts are themselves bound by s 6.

parts.heading: Campbell: the collision opens in London
parts.voice: two rights collide — narrates the first battle in the sequence
body: Naomi Campbell had publicly denied using drugs. The Mirror published a story confirming she was receiving treatment for addiction, together with details of the clinic she attended, a photograph taken covertly outside a Narcotics Anonymous meeting, and some detail about the treatment itself. Campbell sued, but crucially did not dispute the newspaper's right to report that she had lied about drug use in the first place — a public figure's public untruths were fair game. Her claim was narrower and sharper: publishing the clinic details and the covert photograph went further than correcting the record required.

The House of Lords agreed, by a bare majority, and in doing so set the modern structure that every privacy claim since has followed. The first question is whether the claimant had a reasonable expectation of privacy in the information — an objective question, asking what a reasonable person in the claimant's position would feel about the material becoming public. If so, the second question is a balancing exercise between the claimant's Article 8 interest and the publisher's Article 10 interest, with neither right enjoying automatic priority over the other.

Notice how narrowly the House of Lords drew the line. Confirming Campbell's drug use (correcting a public lie) survived Article 10 scrutiny easily. The clinic details and the covert photograph did not — they went beyond what was necessary to tell that story and risked deterring her, and others, from seeking treatment. The lesson is a fine-grained one: publication of a true story about a public figure is not an all-or-nothing question. Each additional detail has to earn its place in the balance separately.

components.factsShort: Naomi Campbell, having publicly denied drug use, sued the Mirror over its publication of details of her addiction treatment and a covertly taken photograph outside a Narcotics Anonymous meeting, though she accepted the paper's right to report that she had lied.
components.ratioShort: A claim for misuse of private information asks first whether the claimant had a reasonable expectation of privacy in the information, then balances the claimant's Article 8 interest against the publisher's Article 10 interest, with neither right taking automatic priority.

expanded.facts: Campbell had told the press she did not use drugs, unlike other models. The Mirror published a story revealing this was untrue, that she was attending Narcotics Anonymous, together with details of the frequency and nature of her treatment and a photograph taken covertly as she left a meeting. She sued for breach of confidence, conceding the paper could lawfully report that she had lied but arguing the additional detail and photograph went too far.
expanded.judgmentExtract: A bare 3–2 majority held that the additional information — details of the treatment and the covert photograph — attracted a reasonable expectation of privacy and that publishing it was not justified by the legitimate purpose of correcting Campbell's public denial. The majority stressed that Article 10 did not require this level of intrusive detail to tell a story that could have been told, and largely was told, without it.
expanded.significance: Campbell is the founding modern case for the tort of misuse of private information, converting breach of confidence into a doctrine built directly around Convention rights rather than a prior confidential relationship. Its two-stage structure — reasonable expectation of privacy, then balancing — is the framework every later case in this lesson applies.

interaction.prompt: A magazine publishes a story confirming that a well-known actor, who had publicly denied being in a relationship, is in fact in a relationship — together with a paparazzi photograph of the couple walking on a public street and a detailed description of the interior of the actor's private home, obtained from an anonymous source. Apply the Campbell framework to identify which elements of the story are most likely to survive an Article 8 challenge, and which are not.
factsToOrder: The actor had publicly denied the relationship
The photograph was taken on a public street
The story includes a detailed description of the interior of the actor's private home
The home details came from an anonymous source, not the actor

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, applying reasonable expectation of privacy and balancing to each element in turn
Issue and Rule given; student applies the two-stage test to each fact and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether publishing the fact of the relationship, the street photograph, and the home interior details each attracts liability for misuse of private information.
modelAnswer.rule: Following Campbell, a claim requires (1) a reasonable expectation of privacy in the specific information, and (2) a balancing exercise between Article 8 and Article 10 where neither right has automatic priority; publication correcting a public denial by the claimant weighs heavily in Article 10's favour, but detail going beyond what correction requires weighs back towards Article 8.
modelAnswer.application: Correcting the actor's public denial of the relationship closely mirrors Campbell's own treatment of Naomi Campbell's public lie about drug use — it is likely to survive Article 10 scrutiny. A photograph taken on a public street, showing nothing more than the couple's presence together in public, is also likely to be treated similarly to core reporting of the corrected fact. The home interior details are the closest analogue to Campbell's clinic details and covert photograph: information with no necessary connection to correcting the public record, obtained from an anonymous source rather than anything the actor put into the public domain, and going well beyond what the story required.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The fact of the relationship and the public street photograph are likely to survive an Article 8 challenge as necessary to a story the actor's own public denial made newsworthy; the home interior details are the most vulnerable element and, on a Campbell-style analysis, are likely to attract liability.

parts.heading: The balance itself: how Article 8 and Article 10 are actually weighed
parts.voice: two rights collide — pauses the narrative to examine the mechanism of the fight itself
body: Both Article 8 and Article 10 are qualified rights, and the qualifications matter here as much as the rights themselves. Article 8(2) permits interference with private life where necessary in a democratic society for, among other things, the protection of the rights and freedoms of others — which includes a publisher's Article 10 rights. Article 10(2) permits restrictions on expression necessary for, among other things, protecting the reputation or rights of others — which includes a claimant's Article 8 rights. Each right's own internal limitation clause is what lets the other one in.

The House of Lords in Re S (a case about reporting restrictions in criminal proceedings, decided the same year as Campbell) set out four propositions that now govern any Article 8/Article 10 clash: neither article has precedence over the other; where the values under the two articles are in conflict, an intense focus on the comparative importance of the specific rights being claimed in the individual case is necessary; the justifications for interfering with or restricting each right must be taken into account; and finally, the proportionality test must be applied to each — a structured, fact-specific balancing exercise, not a general rule that privacy beats publication or vice versa.

That 'intense focus on the specific rights being claimed' is the crucial phrase. It rules out shortcuts like 'public figures have no privacy' or 'the press always wins on matters of public interest'. Every case requires the court to identify precisely what private information is at stake and precisely what expressive interest publishing it serves, then weigh those specific interests against each other — not abstract, general versions of 'privacy' and 'free speech'.

components.citation: European Convention on Human Rights, Article 8(2) and Article 10(2)
components.text: Article 8(2): There shall be no interference by a public authority with the exercise of this right except such as is in accordance with the law and is necessary in a democratic society ... for the protection of the rights and freedoms of others. Article 10(2): The exercise of these freedoms ... may be subject to such ... restrictions ... as are ... necessary in a democratic society ... for the protection of the reputation or rights of others.
elements: Each right's own qualification clause permits restriction to protect the other right
Neither article has precedence over the other (Re S)
An intense, fact-specific focus on the comparative importance of the specific rights claimed is required
The proportionality of any interference or restriction must be assessed on both sides

interaction.prompt: According to the Re S propositions applied in privacy-versus-press cases, which of the following correctly describes how Article 8 and Article 10 relate to each other?
options: Article 10 takes precedence whenever the story concerns a public figure or a matter of general interest

Neither article has precedence; courts must give an intense, fact-specific focus to the comparative importance of the specific rights actually claimed, and test the proportionality of any interference on both sides
Article 8 takes precedence whenever the claimant did not consent to publication

parts.heading: Von Hannover (No 2): Strasbourg supplies the criteria
parts.voice: two rights collide — the battle moves to Strasbourg, which arms the domestic courts with sharper tools
body: Princess Caroline of Monaco had spent years litigating against the German press over paparazzi photographs of her in everyday life — skiing, shopping, walking with her children. An earlier Strasbourg ruling in her favour (Von Hannover (No 1)) had found that photographs of a public figure in purely private activities, contributing nothing to a debate of general interest, could breach Article 8 even where domestic law permitted publication. Von Hannover (No 2) returned to Strasbourg over a different set of photographs, published alongside an article about her father's illness, and here the German courts had permitted publication — a decision Strasbourg this time upheld.

What makes Von Hannover (No 2) essential reading isn't the result so much as the structure Strasbourg supplied for reaching it. The Grand Chamber set out a now-standard checklist of factors for balancing Article 8 against Article 10 in publication disputes: whether the material contributes to a debate of general interest; how well known the person concerned is and what the subject matter of the report is; the person's prior conduct in relation to the media; the content, form and consequences of the publication; and, where relevant, the circumstances in which any photograph was taken.

The 'debate of general interest' criterion does real work here, and it is easy to misstate. It doesn't mean 'a topic the public finds interesting' — celebrity gossip is interesting to a great many readers but is not, without more, a matter of general interest in the Convention sense. It means a topic bearing on public life, public institutions, public health or safety, or genuine matters of legitimate public concern. In Von Hannover (No 2) itself, the photographs succeeded in surviving Article 8 scrutiny specifically because they illustrated an article about the Prince's serious illness — itself arguably a matter with some genuine public dimension, given his public constitutional role — not because a princess skiing is inherently newsworthy.

components.label: The Von Hannover (No 2) balancing factors
points: Contribution to a debate of general interest — genuine public concern, not mere public curiosity
How well known the person is, and the subject matter of the report
The person's prior conduct in relation to the media
The content, form and consequences of the publication
The circumstances in which any photograph was taken, including consent

interaction.prompt: Applying the Von Hannover (No 2) factors, in which scenario does the 'debate of general interest' criterion most clearly favour the publisher?
interaction.scenarioA: A newspaper publishes photographs of a well-known actor sunbathing at a private villa, with an article focused entirely on the actor's appearance and holiday location.
interaction.scenarioB: A newspaper publishes photographs of an elected MP attending an undisclosed meeting with a lobbyist whose firm the MP had recently voted to award a public contract, with an article examining the potential conflict of interest.
interaction.explanation: Scenario B concerns the conduct of an elected official in relation to public decision-making — a genuine matter of general interest under Von Hannover (No 2). Scenario A concerns purely private activity of interest to readers as gossip or curiosity, which Von Hannover (No 1) and (No 2) both treat as falling on the Article 8 side of the balance absent some further public dimension.

parts.heading: ZXC: the modern synthesis, and a new starting point
parts.voice: two rights collide — closes the arc by showing how far the doctrine has travelled
body: ZXC was under criminal investigation by a UK law enforcement body for suspected fraud offences connected to his employer's overseas business. He was never charged. Bloomberg published an article, based on a leaked confidential document, identifying him by name and detailing the substance of the investigation against him. He sued for misuse of private information, arguing he had a reasonable expectation of privacy in the fact of the investigation itself.

The Supreme Court agreed, and in doing so stated a clear general proposition rather than leaving the answer to case-by-case reconstruction each time: as a legitimate starting point, a person under criminal investigation has a reasonable expectation of privacy in respect of information relating to that investigation, at least prior to charge. The reasoning draws on the real, serious reputational harm an accusation can cause even where — especially where — no charge ever follows, and on the public interest in law enforcement bodies being able to investigate without triggering premature publicity that a formal charge would not itself require.

ZXC is best read as the point where Campbell's case-by-case balancing and Von Hannover's structured factor list converge into a working default rule for a whole category of case. It does not abolish the balancing exercise — a starting point is not an irrebuttable presumption, and the same Von Hannover factors (does the story serve a genuine public interest, what is the claimant's public role, and so on) can still displace it on the right facts. What ZXC changes is the starting position: pre-charge, the burden effectively sits with the publisher to justify departing from a presumption of privacy, rather than with the claimant to establish one from scratch each time.

Trace the whole arc and the doctrinal journey becomes visible. Campbell built the tool for weighing individual pieces of information. Von Hannover (No 2) supplied a structured checklist of what should go into that weighing. ZXC took a recurring fact pattern — pre-charge criminal suspects — and converted the outcome of that repeated weighing exercise into a stated default, saving future courts (and future claimants) from re-litigating the same balance from zero every time.

components.factsShort: Bloomberg published an article, based on a leaked confidential letter, naming ZXC and detailing a UK law enforcement investigation into him for suspected fraud, before any charge was brought.
components.ratioShort: As a legitimate starting point, a person under criminal investigation has a reasonable expectation of privacy in information about that investigation prior to charge, though this starting point can be displaced by a sufficiently strong countervailing Article 10 interest on the facts.

expanded.facts: ZXC worked for a company under investigation by a UK law enforcement body over suspected international fraud offences. He personally became a suspect but was never charged. Bloomberg obtained a confidential letter of request sent by the law enforcement body to a foreign state seeking information as part of the investigation, and published an article naming ZXC and setting out details drawn from that letter.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Supreme Court upheld the lower courts' finding for ZXC, holding that, as a legitimate starting point, a person under criminal investigation has a reasonable expectation of privacy in respect of information relating to that investigation prior to charge. On the facts, this expectation was not displaced by any sufficient countervailing public interest, particularly given that the information was drawn from a confidential law enforcement document never intended for publication.
expanded.significance: ZXC is the modern synthesis this lesson builds towards: it takes the Campbell/Von Hannover balancing framework and converts a recurring pattern of outcomes into a stated presumptive rule for pre-charge suspects, while leaving the underlying Article 8/Article 10 balancing exercise intact as the mechanism for displacing that presumption on unusual facts.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below from ZXC v Bloomberg LP, highlight the sentence stating the core legal proposition the Supreme Court adopted.
interaction.passage: The Court considered whether a person under criminal investigation could have a reasonable expectation of privacy in that fact before any charge was brought. It held that, as a legitimate starting point, a person under criminal investigation has, prior to charge, a reasonable expectation of privacy in respect of information relating to that investigation. This starting point reflects the seriousness of the reputational harm an accusation can cause even absent any charge, though it remains capable of being displaced where a sufficiently strong countervailing public interest is shown on the facts of a particular case.
interaction.ratioSentence: It held that, as a legitimate starting point, a person under criminal investigation has, prior to charge, a reasonable expectation of privacy in respect of information relating to that investigation.

testPool.prompt: Name the common law tort through which Article 8 privacy claims are brought against private defendants such as newspapers.
acceptableAnswers: tort of misuse of private information
testPool.modelAnswer: Misuse of private information — a tort developed from the equitable action for breach of confidence, reshaped to reflect Article 8 and Article 10 without requiring a prior confidential relationship.

testPool.prompt: Which case founded the modern two-stage structure (reasonable expectation of privacy, then balancing) for misuse of private information claims?
options: Campbell v MGN Ltd
ZXC v Bloomberg LP

testPool.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes English privacy law's statutory basis?
options: The Human Rights Act creates a free-standing statutory tort of invasion of privacy, directly enforceable against any defendant

There is no free-standing statutory privacy tort; Article 8 reaches private disputes indirectly, through the courts' s 6 duty to develop the common law tort of misuse of private information compatibly with Convention rights
Privacy claims against the press can only be brought under the Data Protection Act, never under the Human Rights Act framework
testPool.trapExplanation: The first option is the precise error this lesson is built to correct. The third overcorrects into a different mistake — data protection legislation exists alongside, not instead of, the common law tort discussed here.

testPool.prompt: State the two stages of the test for misuse of private information set out in Campbell v MGN.
acceptableAnswers: reasonable expectation of privacy, then balancing Article 8 against Article 10
testPool.modelAnswer: First, whether the claimant had a reasonable expectation of privacy in the information; second, if so, a balancing exercise between the claimant's Article 8 interest and the publisher's Article 10 interest, with neither right having automatic priority.

testPool.prompt: Put these developments in the order they occurred.
items: Campbell v MGN establishes the two-stage misuse of private information test
Von Hannover v Germany (No 2) sets out Strasbourg's structured balancing factors
ZXC v Bloomberg LP states a starting-point presumption of privacy for pre-charge criminal suspects

testPool.prompt: According to the Re S propositions relied on in this line of cases, which statement is correct?
options: Article 10 has presumptive priority in any dispute involving a media defendant

Neither Article 8 nor Article 10 has precedence over the other; an intense, fact-specific focus on the comparative importance of the specific rights claimed is required, and proportionality must be tested on both sides
Article 8 has presumptive priority wherever the claimant is a private individual rather than a public figure

testPool.prompt: Under the Von Hannover (No 2) 'debate of general interest' criterion, how much weight does the mere fact that a story is interesting to readers (e.g. celebrity gossip, with no wider public dimension) carry towards justifying publication?
sliderLabels: Very little weight on its own
testPool.correctPosition: Very little weight on its own
testPool.explanation: Von Hannover (No 1) and (No 2) both draw a sharp line between a topic the public finds interesting and a genuine debate of general interest bearing on public life, institutions or safety; mere curiosity value carries little independent weight in the balance.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence listing the Von Hannover (No 2) balancing factors.
testPool.passage: The Grand Chamber considered how domestic courts should approach the balance between Article 8 and Article 10 in cases concerning publication of photographs of private individuals. It identified the following as relevant criteria: contribution to a debate of general interest, how well known the person is and the subject of the report, the person's prior conduct, and the content, form and consequences of the publication. Applying these criteria to the facts, the Court found that the German courts had struck a fair balance in permitting publication.
testPool.ratioSentence: It identified the following as relevant criteria: contribution to a debate of general interest, how well known the person is and the subject of the report, the person's prior conduct, and the content, form and consequences of the publication.

testPool.prompt: A local newspaper learns, from an anonymous tip, that a named private individual is currently under police investigation for suspected fraud, though no charge has been brought. Applying ZXC, what is the claimant's starting legal position if the newspaper publishes the story naming him?
options: As a legitimate starting point, he has a reasonable expectation of privacy in the fact of the investigation prior to charge, which the newspaper would need a sufficiently strong countervailing public interest to displace
He has no expectation of privacy at all, since criminal investigations are inherently matters of general public interest
The claim would automatically fail because he is a private individual, not a public figure
testPool.explanation: This is the core ZXC proposition: pre-charge, a starting-point expectation of privacy applies regardless of whether the claimant is a public figure, though it remains rebuttable on sufficiently strong facts.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario most likely to strengthen a reasonable expectation of privacy under the ZXC approach.
testPool.scenarioText: A journalist obtains, from a confidential internal law enforcement document never intended for release, details of an ongoing pre-charge fraud investigation into a named businessman, and publishes the businessman's name alongside those details before any charge is brought.
tappableSpans: a confidential internal law enforcement document never intended for release
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right. The pre-charge timing is the operative fact under ZXC's starting-point rule — the presumption of privacy specifically attaches prior to charge, reflecting the reputational harm an unresolved accusation can cause.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look again for the fact that triggers ZXC's specific starting-point rule, rather than simply describing the investigation. The rule is expressly tied to the pre-charge stage.

testPool.prompt: Applying the Von Hannover (No 2) factors, in which scenario is a claimant's Article 8 interest most likely to prevail over a publisher's Article 10 interest?
testPool.scenarioA: A magazine publishes photographs, taken with consent at an official state function, of a senior elected official meeting foreign dignitaries.
testPool.scenarioB: A magazine publishes photographs, taken covertly with a long-lens camera, of the same official's teenage child at a private medical appointment, with an article discussing the official's family life generally.
testPool.explanation: Scenario A concerns an official's public role, performed in public with consent, and squarely engages a genuine public interest. Scenario B concerns a family member with no public role, at a specifically sensitive private moment, photographed covertly, with no genuine public-interest justification connecting it to the official's public functions — the classic Von Hannover profile for an Article 8 win.

testPool.prompt: An online publisher obtains leaked medical records showing that a professional athlete, who has built a public brand around peak fitness and has a lucrative sponsorship deal on that basis, has a serious but entirely private health condition unrelated to their sport. The publisher argues the story is justified because the athlete's public image is misleading. Analyse whether the athlete is likely to succeed in a misuse of private information claim.
factsToOrder: The information is drawn from leaked medical records
The condition is serious but unrelated to the athlete's sport
The athlete has cultivated a public brand around fitness
The publisher argues correcting a misleading public image justifies publication

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, applying Campbell, Von Hannover and ZXC-style reasoning throughout
Issue and Rule given; student applies facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the athlete has a reasonable expectation of privacy in their medical condition, and if so, whether the publisher's public-interest justification is strong enough to displace it in the Article 8/Article 10 balance.
modelAnswer.rule: Medical information is a paradigm category attracting a reasonable expectation of privacy under Campbell; the Von Hannover (No 2) factors (genuine debate of general interest, the claimant's public role, prior conduct, content and consequences of publication) then determine whether that expectation is outweighed by the publisher's Article 10 interest, with neither right taking automatic priority.
modelAnswer.application: Medical records are close to the core of Article 8 protection, similar to the clinic and treatment details in Campbell itself. Unlike Campbell's correction of a specific public lie, the argument here — that a cultivated public image is generally 'misleading' — is far looser and does not identify a specific false public statement the athlete made about this condition; it more closely resembles the kind of generalised curiosity interest Von Hannover treats as carrying little independent weight, rather than a genuine debate of general interest. The leaked and unrelated nature of the records, and the serious consequences of publication for someone with no public role in relation to their health, both weigh further towards Article 8.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The athlete is likely to succeed: the information attracts a strong expectation of privacy, and the publisher's justification does not amount to the kind of genuine public-interest correction that displaced privacy in Campbell, making an Article 8 outcome the more probable result of the balancing exercise.

testPool.prompt: A news outlet publishes a story naming a suspect who has already been formally charged with an offence and is due to stand trial. Does ZXC's pre-charge starting-point presumption of privacy apply in the same way here?
options: No — ZXC's starting-point rule is expressly tied to the pre-charge stage; once charged, different considerations (including open justice) come into play
Yes — the presumption applies identically at every stage of the criminal process

testPool.prompt: A student argues: 'Since Von Hannover (No 2) lists 'how well known the person is' as a balancing factor, being a celebrity always weakens a person's Article 8 claim.' What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: There is no flaw — fame is always fatal to a privacy claim

The factor is about the relationship between the person's public role and the specific subject matter of the report, not fame in the abstract; a celebrity can still succeed where the story concerns a purely private matter unconnected to their public role, as Campbell itself shows
Von Hannover (No 2) does not actually include this factor
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting shortcut is to treat fame as a generalised discount on privacy rights. Both Campbell (a famous model) and Von Hannover itself (a princess) show that a well-known claimant can still win where the specific information published has no genuine connection to their public role.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating Article 8 as creating a direct statutory claim, or treating 'public interest' as synonymous with 'interesting to the public'. Keep the mechanism precise (indirect horizontal effect through the common law tort) and keep the Von Hannover 'general interest' criterion tied to genuine public concern, not curiosity or fame alone.
